title: Reloop WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce: agents search, compare and reserve one-of-one inventory with human approval.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce: agents search, compare and reserve one-of-one inventory with human approval.

 Inspiration 

 Reloop started with a very ordinary recommerce problem: second-hand inventory is messy. 

 Listing one item is easy. Listing many is slow. Every garment needs identification, sizing, condition assessment, pricing, descriptions, images and publishing. The buyer side is just as messy: every item is one-of-one, sizing varies, condition is subjective, defects matter, and once an item is gone, it is gone. 

 That makes recommerce a strong test case for agentic shopping. A buyer may not want to click through filters. They may simply ask: 

 
 Find me a genuine black leather jacket around UK size 10, in excellent condition, under R1,200. Avoid faux leather and obvious defects. 
 

 A normal storefront struggles with that kind of intent. A browser automation agent can try to infer meaning from the page, but it is still guessing from a human UI. 

 Reloop asks a different question: 

 What if commerce applications exposed trusted, page-defined capabilities directly to AI agents while still requiring explicit human approval for consequential actions? 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we built a focused public implementation of that idea. 

 

 What it does 

 Reloop is a reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce using WebMCP. 

 It demonstrates a complete human-agent commerce flow: 

 
 The agent discovers the tools exposed by the page. 
 The user describes what they want in natural language. 
 The agent searches deterministic one-of-one inventory. 
 It inspects item details such as material, size, condition, price, defects and availability. 
 It compares candidates and recommends the best match with supporting evidence. 
 The human explicitly approves the exact item in natural language. 
 Only then can the write-path reservation tool change demo state. 
 The storefront updates visibly. 
 

 The demo is intentionally narrow: a recommerce storefront with synthetic inventory. The underlying pattern is broader: read and reasoning actions can be agent-friendly, while write actions remain application-controlled and human-approved. 

 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Most AI web interactions still depend on fragile patterns: 

 
 the agent reads arbitrary HTML and guesses what the page means 
 the agent clicks through a UI designed for humans 
 the app has little control over which actions are safe or intended 
 

 WebMCP changes the boundary. 

 In Reloop, the page explicitly registers meaningful commerce capabilities. The agent does not need to scrape the storefront or invent a workflow. It discovers tools that represent the actual tasks a buyer needs: 

 
 search_inventory 
 inspect_item 
 find_best_match 
 compare_items 
 recommend_alternatives 
 reserve_item 
 

 Those tools are not generic database operations. They are application-level capabilities that map to shopping intent. 

 That is why WebMCP matters here: it lets the website describe what an agent can do, while the application keeps authority over business logic, validation and state changes. 

 

 Better user experience 

 For the human, Reloop turns a messy search into a guided conversation. 

 Instead of filtering by imperfect categories, the user can describe the outcome they want. The agent can then do the tedious work: search, inspect, compare, eliminate poor matches and explain why one item is the strongest choice. 

 For the agent, the experience is also better. It receives structured tool responses rather than trying to interpret visual layout, DOM fragments or arbitrary copy. 

 For the application, the experience is safer. The app decides which capabilities exist, how inputs are validated, what evidence is returned, and when a write action is allowed. 

 The result is not autonomous shopping for its own sake. It is a collaboration: 

 the agent reasons, the application enforces, and the human decides. 

 

 What people and agents can do together now 

 Reloop shows a workflow that is difficult to do well with a normal storefront alone: 

 
 express nuanced buyer intent in natural language 
 evaluate one-of-one inventory with inconsistent attributes 
 compare items on fit, condition, material, price and defects 
 preserve the evidence behind a recommendation 
 keep the human in control of irreversible actions 
 update application state only after explicit approval 
 

 That last point matters. 

 The agent is allowed to search, inspect, compare and recommend freely. But reservation is different. reserve_item is the write path, so it requires explicit natural-language approval for the exact SKU in the tool request. A vague instruction such as “Reserve RL-001” is rejected. Approval language such as “I approve RL-001. Please reserve RL-001 for me.” allows the reservation only if the item exists and is still available. 

 The live deployment has been retested with this boundary: “Reserve RL-001.” returns an approval-required response without changing state. “I approve RL-001. Please reserve RL-001 for me.” succeeds and changes the storefront from 23 → 22 available with RL-001 AVAILABLE → RESERVED . 

 

 How we implemented WebMCP 

 The public challenge repository contains a focused Next.js implementation of the WebMCP layer. 

 The demo registers six Reloop Site Tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool exposes a specific commerce capability to the client. The matching and reservation logic remains separate from the protocol boundary so the WebMCP layer acts as the agent-facing interface, not the entire application. 

 The implementation includes: 

 
 a Next.js demo shell 
 deterministic synthetic inventory 
 recommerce matching and reservation logic 
 WebMCP tool registration 
 explicit approval validation for the write-path reservation tool 
 a human-visible storefront state 
 focused tests and verification commands 
 an AGPLv3 open-source license 
 

 The repository README documents the architecture, tool flow, human approval boundary, local setup and verification path. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest design challenge was deciding what the tools should represent. 

 It would have been easy to expose low-level CRUD functions, but that would not show the real promise of WebMCP. We wanted the agent to work with commerce intent, not database plumbing. 

 The second challenge was trust. 

 A shopping assistant that can reserve items without the user’s clear approval is not a better experience. It is just a faster way to make mistakes. We deliberately separated read/reas
